title: Node running .ts via type stripping; erasable syntax only
summary: Node 22.18+ and 23.6+ run a .ts file directly by blanking out its type syntax with spaces: no build step, no tsconfig, no type check. Only erasable syntax survives that, which is exactly what erasableSyntaxOnly makes tsc enforce.

examples.title: What Node does to a .ts file before V8 runs it

annotations.note: This file runs as it is, with no compile step. The interface and the `: City` and `: string` annotations are replaced by spaces, and the default value `upper = false` stays because it is JavaScript. toLocaleUpperCase("tr") maps i to İ and ı to I, giving DİYARBAKIR; plain toUpperCase() would give DIYARBAKIR.

stripTypeScriptTypes from node:module (22.13 and 23.2, a release candidate API) applies the same transformation to a string. Each output line is exactly as long as its input: the non-null `!`, the `as number` and the whole interface become spaces. Node's docs warn that its output may change between Node versions.

The stack frame names line 26 of this file. Because nothing moved, Node needs no source maps for stack traces or breakpoints. esbuild and tsc rewrite the code, so they need source maps to get the same result.
tsc reports TS2741 (property 'plate' is missing). Node never asks, so the call runs and prints "undefined Ankara". The type check is a separate step: your editor, and `tsc --noEmit` in CI.

examples.title: What Node refuses, and the erasable spelling of each

annotations.note: Each entry becomes a real file in the run's temp directory. Loading them with a dynamic import() makes every failure an exception for that file alone. A static import of enum.ts would stop the whole program before its first line ran, because modules are parsed and linked before any of them executes.

An enum makes the compiler emit an object, so Node refuses it. The as-const object plus a type with the same name gives the same `Level.Warn` at the call site. Only the value shows up in the exports below. The type was erased.

`public x` in a constructor's parameter list declares a field and assigns it, which is code the type stripper would have to write. The explicit field is erasable. A namespace with values compiles to an IIFE; a plain module is the modern namespace. A namespace holding only types is still allowed.

types.ts exports nothing at run time. `import { User }` is therefore a value import of a name that doesn't exist, and module linking fails. Node can't tell a type from a value without type information. `import type` is deleted entirely, and verbatimModuleSyntax makes tsc insist on it (TS1484).

Node resolves the specifier exactly as written: no .ts, .js or /index guessing, and no tsconfig paths. Write "./plain.ts". tsc accepts that with rewriteRelativeImportExtensions or allowImportingTsExtensions, and otherwise reports TS5097.

Plumbing for stable output: Node 22 wraps the parser's message in a code frame and Node 24 does not. Messages of other errors (here ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND) contain absolute paths, so only their code is printed.

use_cases: Scripts and small tools (migrations, data fixes, code generators, CI helpers) written in TS and run with `node script.ts`, no build step and no dev dependency
Small services and CLIs where the deployed code is the source tree, checked by `tsc --noEmit` in CI
The Node test runner (`node --test`) over .ts test files
Choosing tsconfig flags for a codebase that must also run under Vite/esbuild: erasableSyntaxOnly plus verbatimModuleSyntax keep one file valid for all of them
strengths: No build step, and unlike ts-node or tsx no package to install: Node is the only dependency, like `go run` needs only the Go toolchain
Stack traces and breakpoints point at the .ts source with no source maps, because types become spaces and nothing moves
Startup stays fast: the parser only finds and blanks out types. It doesn't check them and doesn't read tsconfig, so it never loads the whole program the way tsc does
The rules are the same erasable subset that esbuild, Vite and Deno handle without surprises, so the same file runs everywhere
weaknesses: No type check at all. Unlike `go run`, which refuses to build code with a type error, `node app.ts` runs code that tsc rejects
tsconfig.json is ignored: no paths aliases, no `target` downleveling, no JSX (.tsx files are refused)
No TypeScript inside node_modules: libraries still have to ship compiled JavaScript plus .d.ts files
Older TS codebases full of enums, namespaces and parameter properties need refactoring (or a full transpiler like tsx) before Node runs them

pitfalls.title: Treating `node app.ts` as a type check
pitfalls.detail: Node strips types without reading them. Run `tsc --noEmit` in CI and before commits; in this repo that is `npm run typecheck`.

pitfalls.title: Importing a type without `type`
pitfalls.detail: The import survives stripping, so Node looks for a runtime export that was never there and linking fails with a SyntaxError. Turn on verbatimModuleSyntax so tsc reports TS1484 at the import.

pitfalls.title: Extensionless imports and tsconfig paths
pitfalls.detail: `import "./db"` and `import "@/db"` both fail with ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND. Write the real file name, and for aliases use package.json subpath imports, which must start with #.

pitfalls.title: Expecting tsconfig's target to downlevel new syntax
pitfalls.detail: Node runs the syntax you wrote. `await using f = await open(path)` works on Node 24 but is a SyntaxError on Node 22, whatever tsconfig says. Check the oldest Node version you deploy to.

pitfalls.title: Non-erasable syntax that still compiles with tsc
pitfalls.detail: enum, namespaces with values, parameter properties, `import x = require()` and `<T>value` assertions all compile with plain tsc and fail in Node with ERR_UNSUPPORTED_TYPESCRIPT_SYNTAX. Set erasableSyntaxOnly so tsc reports TS1294 instead.

quiz.q: Which declaration runs under `node app.ts` unchanged?
options: const Level = { Info: "info", Warn: "warn" } as const
quiz.why: The as-const object is plain JavaScript plus an erasable `as const`. The other three make the compiler generate code, so Node throws ERR_UNSUPPORTED_TYPESCRIPT_SYNTAX.

quiz.q: types.ts contains only `export interface User {}`. What does `import { User } from "./types.ts"` do under Node?
options: Linking fails with a SyntaxError: the module does not provide an export named 'User'
User is undefined at run time
quiz.why: Without `type`, the import is a value import. Node has no type information, so it keeps the import, and the interface left no runtime export behind.

quiz.q: Why do stack traces from a stripped .ts file point at the right line and column without source maps?
options: Node generates source maps in memory
Type syntax is replaced by spaces, so every remaining token keeps its position
quiz.why: Stripping blanks out types in place instead of rewriting code, so positions in the JavaScript V8 runs equal positions in your file.

quiz.q: A script has a type error that tsc reports. What does `node script.ts` do?
options: Prints the type error as a warning and runs
quiz.why: Node performs no type checking. Only tsc (or your editor) reports type errors.

body:
## Concept

`node app.ts` works. Since Node 23.6 and 22.18 type stripping is on by default, since
24.3 it no longer prints an experimental warning, and since 24.12 and 25.2 it is
marked stable. (It arrived behind `--experimental-strip-types` in 22.6.) Node parses
the file with a built-in TypeScript parser, replaces every piece of type syntax with
spaces, and hands the result to V8. That is all it does:

- **no type checking**: a file that tsc rejects still runs;
- **no tsconfig.json**: no `paths`, no `target` downleveling, no JSX;
- **no code generation**: only *erasable* syntax is accepted, meaning syntax that
  leaves valid JavaScript behind once it is blanked out.

The constructs that make the compiler generate code (`enum`, namespaces with values,
parameter properties, `import x = require()`) are refused with
`ERR_UNSUPPORTED_TYPESCRIPT_SYNTAX`, and so is the old `<T>value` assertion syntax. tsc
5.8's `erasableSyntaxOnly` flag rejects the same set at edit time (TS1294), so your
editor tells you before Node does.

Module rules follow from "no type information, no tsconfig": a `.ts` file is ESM or
CommonJS according to the nearest package.json `"type"` (`.mts` is always ESM, `.cts`
always CommonJS), import specifiers need their real extension, type-only imports need
`import type`, `.tsx` is unsupported, and Node refuses TypeScript files anywhere under
`node_modules`.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- Go: `go run main.go` compiles and type-checks; one type error and nothing runs. Node is
  the opposite: it runs first, and the check is a separate `tsc --noEmit` you have to
  wire into CI.
- Python: the closest match. CPython ignores type hints and mypy checks them separately.
  The difference is that Python keeps annotations in `__annotations__` at run time, while
  Node deletes them.
- Java: `java Main.java` (the source launcher, Java 11) compiles in memory with full type
  checking. Node does no checking and keeps no class metadata.
- JS/Node: before this, running TS meant a build step or a loader such as ts-node or
  tsx. Those are still the answer for JSX, `paths` aliases or enums; for erasable code,
  plain `node` is enough.
- C/C++: think of a preprocessor that only blanks out text, never expands anything.

## How it works

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  file["app.ts"] --> resolve["resolve the specifier exactly as written"]
  resolve --> nm{"under node_modules?"}
  nm -- yes --> refuse["refused"]
  nm -- no --> parse["TS parser (WebAssembly)"]
  parse --> erasable{"only erasable syntax?"}
  erasable -- no --> err["ERR_UNSUPPORTED_TYPESCRIPT_SYNTAX"]
  erasable -- yes --> blank["types replaced by spaces"]
  blank --> v8["V8 runs the JavaScript"]
```

Node's own docs recommend TypeScript 5.8 or newer with this tsconfig, and every flag
in it mirrors one runtime rule:

```json
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "noEmit": true,
    "target": "esnext",
    "module": "nodenext",
    "rewriteRelativeImportExtensions": true,
    "erasableSyntaxOnly": true,
    "verbatimModuleSyntax": true
  }
}
```

- `erasableSyntaxOnly`: TS1294 on enum, value namespaces, parameter properties and `<T>x`.
- `verbatimModuleSyntax`: TS1484 when a type is imported without `type`.
- `module: nodenext`: TS2835 when a relative import has no extension.
- `rewriteRelativeImportExtensions` (TS 5.7): allows `./db.ts` specifiers, and rewrites
  them to `.js` if you ever compile instead of strip.

tsc 7.0.2 reports each of these codes for the snippets in example 2.

## Design notes

Running TypeScript directly splits the toolchain into two independent jobs. Node
executes, and tsc is your test suite for types. Keep `tsc --noEmit` in CI; without it
nothing ever checks the types. Write only erasable syntax even where a bundler would
accept more. The rule costs little (literal unions instead of enums, explicit fields
instead of parameter properties, modules instead of namespaces), and in return the same
file runs unchanged under Node, esbuild, Vite, Deno and Bun, and the JavaScript that
executes is your code minus its types. The boundary is publishing: a package on npm
still ships compiled `.js` plus `.d.ts`, because Node won't strip types inside
`node_modules` and consumers may run older Node versions.

expected.erasable-only:
enum.ts          ERR_UNSUPPORTED_TYPESCRIPT_SYNTAX
                 TypeScript enum is not supported in strip-only mode
as-const.ts      ok, exports: Level
param-prop.ts    ERR_UNSUPPORTED_TYPESCRIPT_SYNTAX
                 TypeScript parameter property is not supported in strip-only mode
field.ts         ok, exports: Point
namespace.ts     ERR_UNSUPPORTED_TYPESCRIPT_SYNTAX
                 TypeScript namespace declaration is not supported in strip-only mode
plain.ts         ok, exports: R
types.ts         ok, exports: (nothing)
value-import.ts  SyntaxError
                 The requested module './types.ts' does not provide an export named 'User'
type-import.ts   ok, exports: (nothing)
no-ext.ts        ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND
